name: Tunisia
highestPoint: Jebel ech Chambi (1,544 m)
lowestPoint: Chott el Djerid (-17 m endorheic salt lake)
longestRiver: Medjerda River (450 km, sole perennial river, agricultural lifeline)
majorLakes: Chott el Djerid (vast shimmering Sahara salt flat)
climate: Mediterranean along northern and coastal zones with mild rainy winters and warm dry summers; semi-arid steppe across central plains; arid to hyper-arid desert in the southern Sahara
naturalHazards: Periodic seasonal flash flooding in coastal wadis
Sirocco (hot dry Saharan wind)
Prolonged agricultural droughts
environmentalIssues: Soil erosion and desertification in southern margins
biodiversity: Ichkeul National Park (vital Mediterranean wetland stopover for hundreds of thousands of migrating waterbirds, geese, and storks) and Bou-Hedma National Park
languages: French (widely used in commerce, administration, higher education)
legislature: Assembly of the Representatives of the People (ARP) and National Council of Regions and Districts
mainPoliticalParties: Parliamentary blocs supporting presidential institutional reforms; Echaâb Movement; Democratic Current; Free Destourian Party
latestElections: Presidential election October 6, 2024 (Kaïs Saïed re-elected with 90.7% of the vote); parliamentary elections 2022/2023; next presidential election scheduled 2029
politicalSituation: Consolidated presidential system under President Kaïs Saïed; implementation of the 2022 Constitution; major focus on state-led anti-corruption, public enterprise reform, agricultural food security, and green hydrogen energy exports to Europe.
foreignRelations: Member of Arab League (former headquarters host), African Union, Arab Maghreb Union, Francophonie, OIC, UN; strategic economic association agreement with the European Union (Italy, France, Germany).
military: Tunisian Armed Forces comprising Army, Navy, and Air Force.
adminDivisions: 24 governorates (wilayat)
history: Heartland of the Phoenician Carthaginian Empire founded by Queen Dido (Elyssa) in 814 BC, which rivaled Rome during the Punic Wars under legendary military genius Hannibal Barca. Conquered by Rome in 146 BC, becoming the wealthy province of Africa Proconsularis, producing monumental Roman amphitheatres (El Djem) and mosaics. Arab-Muslim expansion established Kairouan in 670 AD as the first Islamic city in North Africa, building the Great Mosque of Kairouan. Flourished under Aghlabid, Fatimid, and Hafsid Dynasties. Ottoman rule began in 1574 under the Beys of Tunis. French protectorate imposed in 1881. Independence achieved in 1956 under Habib Bourguiba, who championed women's rights (promulgating the revolutionary Code of Personal Status outlawing polygamy). Zine El Abidine Ben Ali ruled from 1987 until the historic 2010–2011 Jasmine Revolution that ignited the Arab Spring. Kaïs Saïed was elected president in 2019.
recentEvents2020_2026: Conducted the October 2024 presidential election affirming Kaïs Saïed's mandate; enacted the ELMED undersea electricity interconnector linking Tunisia to Italy; achieved record olive oil export revenues cementing position as world's #1 non-EU exporter; advanced green hydrogen transit corridors with Germany.
historicalFigures: Ibn Khaldun (Father of sociology, historiography, and modern economics, born in Tunis in 1332)
education: University of Tunis El Manar; University of Carthage; Zitouna University (one of the oldest centers of Islamic learning in the world); high proportion of female engineering and science graduates.
healthcare: Charles Nicolle Hospital and Rabta Hospital in Tunis; advanced medical infrastructure making Tunisia the leading medical tourism hub in North Africa.
socialCustoms: Café culture in seaside Sidi Bou Said and medinas, family couscous gatherings, hammam rituals, wedding jasmine bouquets (Machmoum) worn behind the ear.
etiquette: Friendly greetings with double cheek kisses among same gender, polite inquiries, removing shoes when entering traditional carpeted salons.
nationalIdentity: Defined by Carthaginian antiquity, Hannibal's courage, Ibn Khaldun's intellectual foundation, exemplary Arab-world legal rights for women, and Mediterranean aesthetic beauty.
sectors: Services & Tourism 62%, Industry & Manufacturing 28%, Agriculture & Fishing 10%
industries: Electrical wiring, automotive components, and aerospace manufacturing
Olive oil processing (world's second largest exporter of extra virgin olive oil)
agriculture: Olives and olive oil (over 100 million olive trees nationwide)
Dates (world-renowned Deglet Nour dates from Tozeur and Kebili oases)
naturalResources: Crude petroleum and natural gas (offshore Gulf of Gabès)
energy: Expansion of utility-scale solar farms (Tozeur, Tataouine) and the ELMED 600 MW undersea electrical interconnector connecting Tunisia directly to the European power grid in Sicily
tourism: Premier Mediterranean cultural and resort destination exceeding 9 million visitors annually: whitewashed blue village of Sidi Bou Said, ruins of ancient Carthage, colossal Roman Amphitheatre of El Djem, troglodyte cave dwellings of Matmata (Star Wars filming sets in Tataouine), island of Djerba, and sandy resorts of Hammamet and Sousse.
employment: Automotive and aerospace components, tourism and hospitality, agriculture and olive harvesting, civil service, IT services.
debtInflation: Macroeconomic stabilization supported by robust olive oil export windfalls, tourism recovery, and prudent policy by the Central Bank of Tunisia.
transport: Modern multi-lane toll highway network connecting Bizerte to Gabès; SNCFT passenger rail network; ELMED Mediterranean energy cable; deepwater Port of Rades and Enfidha.
cuisine: Couscous au poisson (national dish: steamed semolina grains served with fresh Mediterranean grouper, potatoes, squash, and spiced broth), Harissa (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: spicy red chili paste blended with garlic, caraway, coriander, and olive oil, served with every meal), Brik à l'oeuf (crispy deep-fried warka pastry parcel filled with whole egg, tuna, capers, parsley, and lemon), Ojja / Shakshouka with spicy Merguez sausage, Lablabi (rich, comforting hot chickpea soup poured over torn stale crusty bread, topped with poached egg, cumin, olive oil, and harissa), Makroudh (semolina pastries stuffed with date paste, fried and dipped in honey and orange blossom syrup), Mint tea with pine nuts.
festivals: Carthage International Festival (ancient Roman amphitheatre music and theatre festival)
Carthage Film Festival (JCC, oldest African and Arab film festival)
music: Malouf (classical Arab-Andalusian orchestral music featuring oud, violin, and kanun), Mezwed (traditional bagpipe folk rhythm), modern stars like Lotfi Bouchnak, Anouar Brahem (oud jazz master), Dhafer Youssef, Emel Mathlouthi.
dance: Raqs traditional folk dance, Stambeli spiritual trance dance.
art: Roman mosaic conservation (Bardo National Museum houses the world's largest collection of Roman mosaics), painted Nabeul ceramic pottery, blue-and-white wrought iron birdcages of Sidi Bou Said.
architecture: Whitewashed Andalusian villas with brilliant cobalt blue doors and mashrabiya lattice windows in Sidi Bou Said; Roman Amphitheatre of El Djem (third largest Roman amphitheatre in the world); Great Mosque of Kairouan; ancient underground troglodyte homes in Matmata.
literature: Ibn Khaldun (The Muqaddimah), Abou el Kacem Chebbi (Will to Life: 'If a people one day wills to live, destiny must surely respond'), Mahmoud Messadi, Hélé Béji.
cinema: Férid Boughedir (Halfaouine: Boy of the Terraces), Moufida Tlatli (The Silences of the Palace), Kaouther Ben Hania (The Man Who Sold His Skin, Oscar-nominated; Four Daughters, Oscar-nominated and Cannes winner 2023); filming location for Star Wars (Luke Skywalker's home planet Tatooine named after Tataouine) and The English Patient.
sports: Tennis: Ons Jabeur ('Minister of Happiness', 3-time Grand Slam finalist: Wimbledon 2022, 2023, US Open 2022, highest-ranked African and Arab player in tennis history), Swimming: Ahmed Hafnaoui (Olympic Gold Medalist Tokyo 2020 & double World Champion) and Oussama Mellouli (2-time Olympic Gold Medalist), Football (Eagles of Carthage: 6-time World Cup participants, 2004 AFCON champions; Espérance de Tunis 4-time CAF Champions League winners).
media: La Presse de Tunisie, Le Temps, Mosaique FM, Télévision Tunisienne (Wataniya 1 & 2), Nessma TV.
clothing: Chechia (traditional crimson felt cylindrical woolen cap, the national headwear crafted by master chaouachis in the souks of Tunis); Jebba (embroidered silk and wool tunic for men); Sefsari (traditional white silk veil wrap worn by women).
crafts: Handcrafted red felt Chechia hats, hand-painted ceramic pottery from Nabeul, woven kilim rugs from Kairouan, hand-blown glass, olive wood carvings.
worldHeritageSites: Punic Town of Kerkuane and its Necropolis
Djerba: Testimony to a settlement pattern in an island territory (inscribed 2023)
unescoIntangible: Harissa, knowledge, skills and culinary and social practices (inscribed 2022)
Pottery skills of the women of Sejnane
Charfia fishing in the Kerkennah Islands
flagDescription: A red field bearing in the center a white circle containing a red crescent partially encircling a red five-pointed star (closely related to the historical Ottoman flag and adopted in 1827 by Al-Husayn II ibn Mahmud, making it one of the oldest national flags in continuous use).
coatOfArmsDescription: Features a golden shield displaying a Punic galley navigating the sea (freedom), a black lion holding a sword (order), and a pair of scales (justice), with the national motto inscribed on a scroll beneath a crescent and star.
travelNotes: A Mediterranean dream destination combining Roman majesty, seaside French-Andalusian charm, and Sahara desert adventures; delicious cuisine; safe and warm hospitality; Ons Jabeur's matches are celebrated nationwide.
shortSummary: Tunisia is the Mediterranean jewel of ancient Carthage and Hannibal, celebrated for the world-renowned Roman mosaics of the Bardo, the whitewashed blue terraces of Sidi Bou Said, UNESCO-honored fiery Harissa, and global tennis champion Ons Jabeur.
geography: Highest point: Jebel ech Chambi (1,544 m). Lowest point: Chott el Djerid (-17 m endorheic salt lake). Longest river: Medjerda River (450 km, sole perennial river, agricultural lifeline). Climate: Mediterranean along northern and coastal zones with mild rainy winters and warm dry summers; semi-arid steppe across central plains; arid to hyper-arid desert in the southern Sahara. Biodiversity: Ichkeul National Park (vital Mediterranean wetland stopover for hundreds of thousands of migrating waterbirds, geese, and storks) and Bou-Hedma National Park.
economy: Sectors: Services & Tourism 62%, Industry & Manufacturing 28%, Agriculture & Fishing 10%. Key industries: Electrical wiring, automotive components, and aerospace manufacturing, Olive oil processing (world's second largest exporter of extra virgin olive oil), Textile and high-end apparel manufacturing, Phosphate mining and chemical fertilizers (Gafsa), Electronics and software engineering, Pharmaceutical manufacturing, Mediterranean beach and cultural tourism. Natural resources: Phosphate rock (Gafsa basin), Crude petroleum and natural gas (offshore Gulf of Gabès), Iron ore, Zinc, Salt, Exceptional solar and wind irradiance. Major exports: Electrical and electronic equipment, Extra virgin olive oil, Apparel and textiles, Deglet Nour dates, Phosphates and chemical fertilizers, Automotive wiring harnesses.
culture: Cuisine: Couscous au poisson (national dish: steamed semolina grains served with fresh Mediterranean grouper, potatoes, squash, and spiced broth), Harissa (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: spicy red chili paste blended with garlic, caraway, coriander, and olive oil, served with every meal), Brik à l'oeuf (crispy deep-fried warka pastry parcel filled with whole egg, tuna, capers, parsley, and lemon), Ojja / Shakshouka with spicy Merguez sausage, Lablabi (rich, comforting hot chickpea soup poured over torn stale crusty bread, topped with poached egg, cumin, olive oil, and harissa), Makroudh (semolina pastries stuffed with date paste, fried and dipped in honey and orange blossom syrup), Mint tea with pine nuts.. Music & Dance: Malouf (classical Arab-Andalusian orchestral music featuring oud, violin, and kanun), Mezwed (traditional bagpipe folk rhythm), modern stars like Lotfi Bouchnak, Anouar Brahem (oud jazz master), Dhafer Youssef, Emel Mathlouthi.. Sports: Tennis: Ons Jabeur ('Minister of Happiness', 3-time Grand Slam finalist: Wimbledon 2022, 2023, US Open 2022, highest-ranked African and Arab player in tennis history), Swimming: Ahmed Hafnaoui (Olympic Gold Medalist Tokyo 2020 & double World Champion) and Oussama Mellouli (2-time Olympic Gold Medalist), Football (Eagles of Carthage: 6-time World Cup participants, 2004 AFCON champions; Espérance de Tunis 4-time CAF Champions League winners).. Festivals: Carthage International Festival (ancient Roman amphitheatre music and theatre festival), Carthage Film Festival (JCC, oldest African and Arab film festival), International Festival of the Sahara (Douz), Kairouan Mawlid Festival.

name: Uganda
highestPoint: Margherita Peak on Mount Stanley in the Rwenzori Mountains (5,109 m)
lowestPoint: Albert Nile at the South Sudan border (614 m)
longestRiver: Victoria Nile / Albert Nile (source of the Nile River at Jinja flowing north)
majorLakes: Lake Victoria (second largest freshwater lake in the world, 45% in Uganda)
majorMountains: Rwenzori Mountains (legendary snow-capped 'Mountains of the Moon')
Mount Elgon (4,321 m extinct shield volcano)
Virunga Volcanoes (Mount Muhavura, Mount Gahinga, Mount Sabyinyo)
climate: Equatorial highland with abundant year-round rainfall and two wet seasons (March–May, September–November); pleasantly warm and spring-like year-round due to high plateau elevation ('The Pearl of Africa')
naturalHazards: Localized landslides on steep slopes of Mount Elgon during heavy rains
Periodic flash flooding in low-lying river plains
environmentalIssues: Deforestation and wetland drainage for agriculture
Soil erosion in highland farming areas
Lake Victoria water hyacinth and pollution control
biodiversity: Named by Winston Churchill as 'The Pearl of Africa': Bwindi Impenetrable National Park (harboring nearly half of the world's remaining endangered mountain gorillas), Queen Elizabeth National Park (tree-climbing lions and Kazinga Channel boat safaris), and Murchison Falls National Park
languages: English (official language of government, education, and courts)
Luganda (dominant language of the central region)
mainPoliticalParties: National Unity Platform (NUP, led by Robert Kyagulanyi / Bobi Wine)
latestElections: General election 2021; presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled early 2026
politicalSituation: Governed by President Yoweri Museveni since 1986; major infrastructure focus on completing the East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP) and Lake Albert petroleum extraction (Tilenga and Kingfisher fields), alongside regional mediation in the Great Lakes.
foreignRelations: Member of East African Community (EAC), African Union, Commonwealth, IGAD, OIC, UN; hosted the 19th Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) Summit and G77+China Summit in Kampala in January 2024; leading troop contributor to ATMIS in Somalia.
military: Uganda Peoples' Defence Forces (UPDF).
adminDivisions: 4 administrative regions divided into 135 districts and the capital city of Kampala
history: Inhabited by hunter-gatherers, then agriculturalists and pastoralists who formed powerful centralized kingdoms: the Kingdom of Buganda (ruled by the Kabaka), Bunyoro-Kitara, Ankole, Toro, and Busoga. Arab merchants arrived in the 1840s, followed by British explorers John Hanning Speke (who identified the Source of the Nile at Jinja in 1862) and Henry Morton Stanley. British established the Uganda Protectorate in 1894. Gained independence in 1962 under Prime Minister Milton Obote with Kabaka Mutesa II as ceremonial president. Idi Amin seized power in a 1971 military coup, unleashing eight years of terror, economic devastation, and the expulsion of 80,000 Ugandan Asians. Amin was ousted in 1979 by Tanzanian forces and Ugandan exiles. Following civil conflict, the National Resistance Army (NRA) led by Yoweri Museveni took power in 1986, launching decades of economic recovery.
recentEvents2020_2026: Hosted the 19th Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) Summit and South Summit in Kampala in 2024; mobilized full construction of the 1,443 km East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP) linking Lake Albert oilfields to Tanzania's port of Tanga; commissioned the 600 MW Karuma Hydroelectric Dam on the Nile; celebrated Olympic and World distance running dominance (Joshua Cheptegei, Jacob Kiplimo).
religions: Christianity (Roman Catholic ~39.3%, Anglican / Church of Uganda ~32.0%, Pentecostal ~11.1%) ~84.5%
education: Makerere University in Kampala (one of Africa's most prestigious and historic academic institutions, celebrating over a century of scholarship); Kyambogo University; Mbarara University of Science and Technology; universal primary education (UPE).
healthcare: Mulago National Referral Hospital in Kampala; Uganda Heart Institute; Uganda Cancer Institute; world-renowned pioneer in overcoming HIV/AIDS through open public awareness (ABC model).
socialCustoms: Kwanjula (traditional Buganda introduction and engagement ceremony), Rolex street snack culture, communal matooke peeling, passionate enthusiasm for football and music.
etiquette: Kneeling slightly when greeting elders (among women in Buganda culture), gentle two-handed handshakes, warm inquiries after family welfare, soft-spoken manners.
nationalIdentity: Celebrated as 'The Pearl of Africa', defined by the mist-shrouded mountain gorillas of Bwindi, the Source of the Nile, glorious royal kingdom heritage, and world distance running champions.
industries: Petroleum extraction and pipeline infrastructure (Tilenga and Kingfisher Lake Albert oilfields, EACOP)
Coffee processing and roasting (top African coffee exporter)
Cement and steel manufacturing (Tororo, Roofings Group)
Beverage brewing and distilling (Nile Breweries / Nile Special, Uganda Breweries / Bell Lager)
Food processing and sugar refining (Kakira, Lugazi)
agriculture: Coffee (Robusta native to Uganda, Arabica on Mount Elgon - top coffee exporter in Africa)
Bananas / Matooke (second largest producer in the world)
naturalResources: Crude petroleum (over 6.5 billion barrels in Lake Albert basin)
energy: Abundant green clean electricity from the Nile: Karuma Hydroelectric Dam (600 MW), Bujagali Dam, and Isimba Dam generating massive surplus power exported to Kenya, Rwanda, and South Sudan
tourism: World-class primate and wildlife adventure tourism: trekking endangered mountain gorillas in Bwindi Impenetrable Forest and Mgahinga, viewing tree-climbing lions in Ishasha (Queen Elizabeth National Park), white-water rafting the rapids of the Nile at Jinja, hiking the snow-capped Rwenzori Mountains, and boat cruises to the base of Murchison Falls.
employment: Over 68% in smallholder agriculture (coffee, tea, matooke), informal commerce in Kampala, tourism and hospitality, construction.
debtInflation: Macroeconomic stability backed by Bank of Uganda independent inflation-targeting framework; stable Ugandan Shilling.
transport: Modern Entebbe-Kampala Expressway; Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) connection projects; Port Bell and Jinja lake freight links on Lake Victoria; expanded Entebbe International Airport.
airports: Entebbe International Airport (EBB, on the shores of Lake Victoria)
ports: Landlocked; primary oceanic freight access through Port of Mombasa (Kenya, via Northern Corridor) and Port of Dar es Salaam (Tanzania, via Central Corridor)
cuisine: Rolex (legendary Ugandan street food: warm rolled chapati wrapped around a freshly fried vegetable omelet with diced tomatoes, onions, and cabbage—'rolled eggs' / Rolex), Matooke (green cooking bananas steamed in banana leaves, mashed into a smooth golden mound, served with rich beef, chicken, or groundnut peanut sauce), Luwombo (royal Buganda dish: chicken, beef, or smoked fish with mushrooms and peanut sauce wrapped and slow-steamed inside banana leaves), Posho (cornmeal porridge), Malewa (smoked bamboo shoots from Mount Elgon cooked in peanut sauce), Roasted gonja (sweet plantains), Nile Special beer.
festivals: Nyege Nyege Festival (internationally celebrated 4-day electronic and traditional African music festival in Jinja)
Martyrs' Day (June 3, pilgrimage of millions to Namugongo Shrine)
music: Kadongo Kamu (traditional acoustic guitar storytelling music), modern Ugandan Afro-beat, dancehall, and R&B (Bobi Wine, Eddy Kenzo Grammy nominee and BET Award winner, Jose Chameleone, Bebe Cool, Sheebah Karungi, Vinka).
dance: Bakisimba (graceful royal Buganda court dance mimicking the swaying of banana trees and drunk royal steps), Bwola royal Acholi dance, Runyege courtship dance.
art: Barkcloth making (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: ancient craft of harvesting and beating the inner bark of the Mutuba fig tree into soft terracotta-colored cloth), woven raffia peace baskets, soapstone and wood carvings.
architecture: Kasubi Tombs (UNESCO World Heritage: monumental circular thatched royal burial palace of the Buganda Kings); Uganda Martyrs Shrine at Namugongo; colonial architecture at Makerere University.
literature: Okot p'Bitek (Song of Lawino, monumental African classic), Jennifer Nansubuga Makumbi (Kintu, The First Woman), Moses Isegawa (Abyssinian Chronicles).
cinema: Queen of Katwe (starring Lupita Nyong'o and David Oyelowo, filmed in Kampala), Wakaliwood (ultra-low-budget DIY gonzo action cinema in the slums of Wakaliga: Who Killed Captain Alex?); Uganda Film Festival.
sports: Long-distance athletics world supremacy: Joshua Cheptegei (10,000m Olympic Gold Medalist Paris 2024, 5,000m Olympic Gold Tokyo 2020, 5,000m and 10,000m World Record Holder, 3-time World Champion), Jacob Kiplimo (Half-Marathon World Record Holder & World Cross Country Champion), Peruth Chemutai (Olympic Gold 3000m Steeplechase Tokyo 2020 & Silver Paris 2024), John Akii-Bua (1972 Olympic 400m Hurdles Gold and World Record), Football (Uganda Cranes).
media: New Vision, Daily Monitor, NBS Television, NTV Uganda, Bukedde.
clothing: Gomesi / Busauti (striking formal floor-length dress with exaggerated pointed shoulders, square neckline, and a wide silk sash tied around the waist, worn by women); Kanzu white robe worn by men with a tailored suit jacket.
crafts: Barkcloth textiles, woven banana fiber and raffia baskets, carved wooden gorilla sculptures, musical instruments (Adungu arched harp).
worldHeritageSites: Tombs of Buganda Kings at Kasubi
unescoIntangible: Barkcloth making in Uganda (inscribed 2008)
Bigwala, gourd trumpet music and dance of the Busoga Kingdom
Empaako naming system
famousPeople: Joshua Cheptegei (Olympic Champion & World Record Holder)
flagDescription: Six equal horizontal bands of black (the African people), yellow (the bright African sunshine), and red (the brotherhood of all mankind), repeated twice, with a white disk in the center bearing a Grey Crowned Crane (the national bird, facing the hoist).
coatOfArmsDescription: Features a shield and crossed spears over the green slopes of the Rwenzori mountains and source of the Nile, supported by a Kob antelope and a Grey Crowned Crane, depicting a drum, sun, and Nile waters, above the motto 'For God and My Country'.
travelNotes: Earns its legendary title 'The Pearl of Africa' with lush green beauty, warm spring-like climate, and unmatched wildlife safaris; tracking mountain gorillas in Bwindi is life-changing; tasting a freshly made street Rolex is a national rite of passage.
shortSummary: Uganda is Winston Churchill's legendary 'Pearl of Africa', an equatorial paradise blessed with the mist-shrouded mountain gorillas of Bwindi, the roaring Source of the Nile at Jinja, the snow-capped Rwenzori Mountains of the Moon, and Olympic distance running champions like Joshua Cheptegei.

Natural resources: Crude petroleum (over 6.5 billion barrels in Lake Albert basin), Arable fertile volcanic soils, Hydropower on the Nile River, Gold, Copper and cobalt (Kilembe), Iron ore, Limestone and phosphates. Sports: Long-distance athletics world supremacy: Joshua Cheptegei (10,000m Olympic Gold Medalist Paris 2024, 5,000m Olympic Gold Tokyo 2020, 5,000m and 10,000m World Record Holder, 3-time World Champion), Jacob Kiplimo (Half-Marathon World Record Holder & World Cross Country Champion), Peruth Chemutai (Olympic Gold 3000m Steeplechase Tokyo 2020 & Silver Paris 2024), John Akii-Bua (1972 Olympic 400m Hurdles Gold and World Record), Football (Uganda Cranes).. Festivals: Nyege Nyege Festival (internationally celebrated 4-day electronic and traditional African music festival in Jinja), Rolex Festival (Kampala), Independence Day (October 9), Martyrs' Day (June 3, pilgrimage of millions to Namugongo Shrine).

name: Zambia
nationalAnthem: Stand and Sing of Zambia, Proud and Free
highestPoint: Unnamed peak in the Mafinga Hills (2,339 m)
longestRiver: Zambezi River (2,574 km total, giving the country its name) / Kafue River / Luangwa River
majorLakes: Lake Kariba (one of the world's largest man-made reservoirs by volume)
Lake Bangweulu (wetland haven for shoebill storks)
climate: Tropical modified by elevation into pleasant subtropical highland conditions; rainy season from November to April; cool dry winter from May to August; hot dry spring from September to October
naturalHazards: Periodic severe droughts impacting hydroelectric generation
Localized seasonal flash flooding in low-lying river plains
environmentalIssues: Heavy reliance on hydropower vulnerable to regional droughts
Mining pollution and soil degradation in the historic Copperbelt
biodiversity: South Luangwa National Park (one of the greatest wildlife sanctuaries in Africa, home to walking safaris, leopards, and Thornicroft's giraffes), Kafue National Park, and Lower Zambezi National Park
languages: English (official language of government, education, and commerce)
Bemba (widely spoken in Lusaka and Copperbelt, ~33%)
latestElections: Historic general election August 2021 (Hakainde Hichilema won a landslide democratic opposition victory); next scheduled 2026
politicalSituation: Model of peaceful democratic alternation in Southern Africa; successful completion of landmark sovereign debt restructuring under the G20 Common Framework in 2024; economic resurgence driving massive investments in copper mining toward a national goal of 3 million tonnes annual production by 2031.
foreignRelations: Member of SADC, COMESA (headquarters host in Lusaka), African Union, Commonwealth, UN; historic champion of liberation struggles across Southern Africa; strategic partnerships with US, EU, China, and regional neighbors.
military: Zambian Defence Force (ZDF) comprising Army, Air Force, and National Service.
adminDivisions: 10 provinces
history: Inhabited by San hunter-gatherers, followed by Bantu migrations in the 12th–15th centuries establishing kingdoms such as the Maravi, Lunda, and Bemba, and the Barotseland Kingdom of the Lozi. David Livingstone reached the colossal waterfalls on the Zambezi in 1855, naming them Victoria Falls after the British monarch. Administered by Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company (BSAC), then declared the British protectorate of Northern Rhodesia in 1924. Discovery of the immense Copperbelt in the late 1920s drove rapid mining development and trade union activism. Kenneth Kaunda ('KK') led the United National Independence Party (UNIP) to independence on October 24, 1964, adopting the unifying national motto 'One Zambia, One Nation'. Kaunda governed for 27 years, providing sanctuary and headquarters to liberation movements (ANC, SWAPO, FRELIMO, ZANU) before peacefully conceding defeat in multi-party democratic elections in 1991.
recentEvents2020_2026: Achieved landmark sovereign debt restructuring agreement with bilateral and commercial eurobond creditors under the G20 Common Framework; secured major multi-billion-dollar investments to triple national copper production (Kansanshi, Mopani, Konkola Copper Mines, Mingomba AI-driven copper discovery); mobilized national drought response and expanded solar micro-grids; opened the modernized Kazungula Bridge corridor.
historicalFigures: Kenneth Kaunda (KK, founding father of the nation)
Kalusha Bwalya (1988 African Footballer of the Year)
religions: Christianity (Protestant, Pentecostal, Catholic - constitutionally declared a Christian nation) ~95.5%
education: University of Zambia (UNZA in Lusaka); Copperbelt University (CBU in Kitwe); Mulungushi University (Kabwe); free primary and secondary education policy introduced in 2022.
healthcare: University Teaching Hospital (UTH in Lusaka); Levy Mwanawasa University Teaching Hospital; expanding district hospital infrastructure and community health workers.
socialCustoms: Kuomboka ceremony of the Lozi people (spectacular annual royal voyage moving the Litunga King from the flooded Barotse floodplain to higher ground in a giant black-and-white royal barge paddled by 100 warriors), communal nshima dining, afternoon tea gatherings.
etiquette: Respectful greetings with right hand supported by holding the left elbow, clapping hands gently to show gratitude, showing deep deference to elders and traditional chiefs.
nationalIdentity: Defined by the proud motto 'One Zambia, One Nation', the thunder of Victoria Falls (Mosi-oa-Tunya: 'The Smoke That Thunders'), global copper mining supremacy, and peaceful democratic resilience.
industries: Copper mining and smelting (Kansanshi, Sentinel, Lumwana, Mopani - top African copper producer)
Emerald mining (Kagem mine, world's largest producer of premium emeralds)
Hydropower generation (Kariba North, Kafue Gorge Lower 750 MW)
naturalResources: Copper (world top-tier producer, essential for global electrification)
Hydropower potential on Zambezi and Kafue rivers
energy: Massive hydroelectric assets: Kafue Gorge Lower (750 MW), Kariba North Bank (1,080 MW), expanding utility-scale solar farms (Bangweulu, Ngonye, and Ittezhi-Tezhi solar plants) to counter drought vulnerability
tourism: Premier global safari and natural wonder destination: Victoria Falls (Mosi-oa-Tunya, world's largest sheet of falling water), walking safaris in South Luangwa National Park, canoeing the Lower Zambezi, Devil's Pool infinity swim on the edge of Victoria Falls, and observing the annual fruit bat migration in Kasanka (world's largest mammal migration by number).
employment: Copper mining and contracting, smallholder and commercial agriculture, tourism and safari lodges, civil service.
debtInflation: Macroeconomic resurgence following successful G20 debt restructuring; Kwacha stabilized by the Bank of Zambia; rising copper export windfalls.
transport: TAZARA Railway linking to the Port of Dar es Salaam; Kazungula Bridge over the Zambezi linking to Botswana; Lobito Atlantic Railway corridor (linking the Copperbelt to Angola's Atlantic port); Kenneth Kaunda International Airport.
airports: Kenneth Kaunda International Airport (LUN in Lusaka, modernized passenger terminal)
Harry Mwaanga Nkumbula International Airport (LVI in Livingstone)
Simon Mwansa Kapwepwe International Airport (NLA in Ndola)
ports: Landlocked; primary oceanic freight access through Port of Walvis Bay (Namibia, via Walvis Bay Corridor), Port of Dar es Salaam (Tanzania), Port of Durban (South Africa), and Port of Lobito (Angola)
cuisine: Nshima (the undisputed national staple: thick porridge cooked from white maize meal flour, rolled into balls by hand and dipped into relish), Ifisashi (rich relish of pounded pumpkin leaves, collard greens, or sweet potato leaves cooked with ground peanut powder), T-Bone steak and braised goat meat, Kapenta (tiny freshwater fish from Lake Kariba, dried and fried crispy with onions and tomatoes), Chikanda ('African polony': vegetarian cake made from wild orchid tubers, peanuts, and chili), Roasted maize, Mosi Premium Lager.
festivals: Kuomboka (spectacular Barotse royal barge festival in April)
Nc'wala (first fruits warrior festival of the Ngoni people in Chipata)
music: Kalindula (traditional up-tempo bass-guitar driven dance music: Amayenge, PK Chishala), Zamrock (legendary 1970s psychedelic rock movement blending funk and heavy rock: WITCH / We Intend To Cause Havoc), contemporary Zambian Afro-pop and hip-hop (Macky 2, Slapdee, Yo Maps, Cleo Ice Queen).
dance: Ngoni warrior stomping dance, Makishi masquerade dance (UNESCO heritage), Silimba xylophone dances.
art: Makishi wooden and fiber masquerade masks, handwoven Tonga baskets (Bingwa baskets), copper artwork and repoussé reliefs.
architecture: Colonial brick and veranda architecture in historic Livingstone; traditional thatched royal compounds in Barotseland; modern skyscrapers in Lusaka Central Business District.
literature: Binwell Sinyangwe (A Cowrie of Hope), Dominic Mulaisho (The Tongue of the Dumb), Ellen Banda-Aaku.
cinema: I Am Not a Witch (directed by Zambian-Welsh filmmaker Rungano Nyoni, premiered at Cannes and won BAFTA Award 2018); On Becoming a Guinea Fowl (Rungano Nyoni, won Best Director at Cannes 2024).
sports: Football: Chipolopolo / The Copper Bullets (fairy-tale champions of the 2012 Africa Cup of Nations, honoring the memory of the tragic 1993 national team plane crash off Gabon; legendary African Footballer of the Year Kalusha Bwalya; women's team Copper Queens featuring Olympic hat-trick sensation Barbra Banda), Athletics (Muzala Samukonga, Olympic 400m Bronze Medalist Paris 2024 and Commonwealth Champion).
media: Zambia Daily Mail, Times of Zambia, ZNBC (Zambia National Broadcasting Corporation), Diamond TV, Muvi TV.
clothing: Chitenge (vibrant printed cotton wrap fabric worn around the waist or tailored into elegant dresses and suits); British-style formal business wear.
crafts: Tonga handwoven baskets, copper jewelry and decorative plates, carved wooden walking sticks, Makishi ceremonial masks.
unescoIntangible: Gule Wamkulu (shared with Malawi and Mozambique)
Makishi masquerade
Mooba dance of the Lenje ethnic group
Budima dance
flagDescription: A green field (natural resources and lush vegetation) with an eagle in flight in the upper fly corner in orange, hovering above three vertical stripes on the lower fly corner of red (struggle for freedom), black (the people of Zambia), and orange (mineral wealth, particularly copper).
coatOfArmsDescription: Features an African fish eagle hovering over a shield depicted with wavy black and white vertical lines representing Victoria Falls, supported by a man and a woman in casual attire, with a maize cob, mine shafthead, and zebra, over the motto 'One Zambia, One Nation'.
travelNotes: One of Africa's safest, most peaceful, and wildlife-rich countries; home of the original walking safari; swimming in Devil's Pool atop Victoria Falls is a bucket-list thrill.
shortSummary: Zambia is the proud copper-rich powerhouse of Southern Africa, celebrated for the roaring grandeur of Victoria Falls ('The Smoke That Thunders'), pristine walking safaris in South Luangwa, and Cannes-winning cinema by Rungano Nyoni.
geography: Highest point: Unnamed peak in the Mafinga Hills (2,339 m). Lowest point: Zambezi River (329 m). Longest river: Zambezi River (2,574 km total, giving the country its name) / Kafue River / Luangwa River. Climate: Tropical modified by elevation into pleasant subtropical highland conditions; rainy season from November to April; cool dry winter from May to August; hot dry spring from September to October. Biodiversity: South Luangwa National Park (one of the greatest wildlife sanctuaries in Africa, home to walking safaris, leopards, and Thornicroft's giraffes), Kafue National Park, and Lower Zambezi National Park.

Natural resources: Copper (world top-tier producer, essential for global electrification), Cobalt, Emeralds (produces over 20% of world supply), Hydropower potential on Zambezi and Kafue rivers, Gold, Nickel, Arable fertile agricultural plateaus. Major exports: Refined copper and cathodes, Rough and cut emeralds, Cobalt, Raw sugar, Soybeans and meal, Tobacco, Electricity.
culture: Cuisine: Nshima (the undisputed national staple: thick porridge cooked from white maize meal flour, rolled into balls by hand and dipped into relish), Ifisashi (rich relish of pounded pumpkin leaves, collard greens, or sweet potato leaves cooked with ground peanut powder), T-Bone steak and braised goat meat, Kapenta (tiny freshwater fish from Lake Kariba, dried and fried crispy with onions and tomatoes), Chikanda ('African polony': vegetarian cake made from wild orchid tubers, peanuts, and chili), Roasted maize, Mosi Premium Lager.. Music & Dance: Kalindula (traditional up-tempo bass-guitar driven dance music: Amayenge, PK Chishala), Zamrock (legendary 1970s psychedelic rock movement blending funk and heavy rock: WITCH / We Intend To Cause Havoc), contemporary Zambian Afro-pop and hip-hop (Macky 2, Slapdee, Yo Maps, Cleo Ice Queen).. Sports: Football: Chipolopolo / The Copper Bullets (fairy-tale champions of the 2012 Africa Cup of Nations, honoring the memory of the tragic 1993 national team plane crash off Gabon; legendary African Footballer of the Year Kalusha Bwalya; women's team Copper Queens featuring Olympic hat-trick sensation Barbra Banda), Athletics (Muzala Samukonga, Olympic 400m Bronze Medalist Paris 2024 and Commonwealth Champion).. Festivals: Kuomboka (spectacular Barotse royal barge festival in April), Independence Day (October 24), Nc'wala (first fruits warrior festival of the Ngoni people in Chipata), Umutomboko (Lunda kingdom ceremony), Likumbi Lya Mize (Luvale festival).

name: Zimbabwe
nationalAnthem: Simudzai Mureza wedu WeZimbabwe (Blessed be the Land of Zimbabwe)
highestPoint: Mount Nyangani (2,592 m in the Eastern Highlands)
lowestPoint: Confluence of Runde and Save Rivers (162 m)
longestRiver: Zambezi River (forms northern border) / Limpopo River (southern border) / Save River
majorLakes: Lake Kariba (one of the world's largest man-made reservoirs)
majorMountains: Eastern Highlands (Nyanga Mountains, Bvumba Mountains, Chimanimani Mountains)
climate: Subtropical highland climate across high plateau (Highveld) with warm wet summers (November–March) and cool dry winters (May–August); hot semi-arid in low-lying Zambezi and Limpopo valleys (Lowveld)
naturalHazards: Recurrent periodic droughts caused by El Niño weather patterns
Tropical cyclones moving inland from the Mozambique Channel (Cyclone Idai)
Seasonal flash floods
environmentalIssues: Deforestation for firewood and tobacco curing
biodiversity: Hwange National Park (famed for one of the largest elephant populations in the world, over 40,000 elephants), Mana Pools National Park (UNESCO site famed for walking safaris and elephants standing on hind legs to reach acacia pods), and Gonarezhou National Park
languages: 16 official languages recognized by the 2013 Constitution: Shona (~75%), Ndebele (~18%), English (official administrative/business language), Chewa, Chibarwe, Kalanga, Tsoa (Koisan), Nambya, Ndau, Shangani, Sign Language, Sotho, Tonga, Tswana, Venda, Xhosa
currency: Zimbabwe Gold (ZiG - gold-backed currency introduced April 2024) and US Dollar (USD, $ co-circulating)
legislature: Parliament of Zimbabwe (Senate and National Assembly)
mainPoliticalParties: ZANU-PF (Zimbabwe African National Union – Patriotic Front)
latestElections: General election August 2023 (Emmerson Mnangagwa re-elected president; ZANU-PF parliamentary majority); next scheduled 2028
politicalSituation: President Emmerson Mnangagwa second term; implementation of 'Vision 2030' to attain upper-middle-income status; introduced the gold-backed ZiG currency in 2024 to curb hyperinflation; massive expansion in lithium extraction and battery-grade processing.
foreignRelations: Member of SADC (chaired SADC summit in Harare in August 2024), African Union, UN; strategic partnerships with China, Russia, UAE, and regional Southern African neighbors; active re-engagement with the Commonwealth.
military: Zimbabwe Defence Forces (ZDF) comprising Zimbabwe National Army and Air Force of Zimbabwe.
adminDivisions: 8 provinces and 2 cities with provincial status (Harare and Bulawayo)
history: Site of the monumental Kingdom of Zimbabwe (11th–15th centuries), centered at Great Zimbabwe, whose dry-stone monumental walls and towers were built without mortar by Shona ancestors. Succeeded by the Kingdom of Mutapa and the Rozvi Empire. In the 1830s, Mzilikazi led the Ndebele (Matabele) migration from Zululand, founding the Matabele Kingdom based at Bulawayo. Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company invaded in 1890, colonizing the territory as Southern Rhodesia. White minority leader Ian Smith issued the Unilateral Declaration of Independence (UDI) in 1965. A protracted liberation war (Second Chimurenga) waged by ZANLA (led by Robert Mugabe) and ZIPRA (led by Joshua Nkomo) culminated in the 1979 Lancaster House Agreement. Recognized independence achieved on April 18, 1980 under Robert Mugabe, who ruled for 37 years until resigning in November 2017, succeeded by Emmerson Mnangagwa.
recentEvents2020_2026: Chaired the 44th SADC Heads of State Summit in Harare in 2024; introduced the gold-backed Zimbabwe Gold (ZiG) currency in April 2024; emerged as Africa's largest lithium producer and banned raw lithium exports to mandate domestic processing; completed the Hwange Thermal Power Station units 7 & 8 expansion (adding 600 MW); expanded the Robert Gabriel Mugabe International Airport.
historicalFigures: Mbuya Nehanda (spiritual leader of the First Chimurenga)
literacyRate: 88.7% (traditionally among the highest literacy rates in Africa)
education: University of Zimbabwe (historic premier institution in Harare); National University of Science and Technology (NUST in Bulawayo); Midlands State University; renowned rigorous secondary educational system (ZIMSEC).
healthcare: Parirenyatwa Group of Hospitals and Harare Central Hospital (Sally Mugabe Hospital); Mpilo Central Hospital in Bulawayo; expanding rural clinic networks.
socialCustoms: Hunhu / Ubuntu philosophy ('Munhu munhu nevanhu' - a person is a person through other people), Roora / Lobola (traditional marriage bride price ceremonies), family gathering around the hearth (Dare), Mbira music spiritual ceremonies (Bira).
etiquette: Respectful greetings with clapping hands (two or three gentle rhythmic claps), receiving items with both hands or holding right wrist, addressing elders with totems (Mitupo).
nationalIdentity: Defined by the monumental stone heritage of Great Zimbabwe, the thunderous spray of Victoria Falls (Mosi-oa-Tunya), the soulful plucking of the Mbira, high academic pride, and the sacred Zimbabwe Bird emblem.
sectors: Agriculture & Forestry 12%, Mining & Heavy Industry 25%, Services 63%
industries: Lithium mining and processing (Bikita, Arcadia - Africa's top lithium producer)
Platinum group metals mining (Zimplats, Mimosa, Unki - second largest reserves in the world)
Flue-cured tobacco processing and leaf auctioning
agriculture: Flue-cured Virginia tobacco (world's top quality tobacco exporter)
Sugarcane (Hippo Valley, Triangle estates in Lowveld)
energy: Hwange Thermal Power Station (recently expanded with units 7 & 8 adding 600 MW), Kariba South Hydroelectric Power Station (1,050 MW), expanding utility solar plants
tradePartners: China (major buyer of tobacco and lithium)
tourism: Premier global tourism destination: Victoria Falls (world's greatest curtain of falling water, UNESCO site), Great Zimbabwe National Monument (colossal medieval stone city), Hwange National Park (elephant kingdom), Mana Pools National Park, canoeing the Zambezi, and hiking the Eastern Highlands (Nyanga, Bvumba).
employment: Smallholder and commercial agriculture, mining contracting, informal commerce, tourism hospitality, civil service.
debtInflation: Monetary stabilization supported by the gold-backed Zimbabwe Gold (ZiG) currency; structured dialogue with international financial institutions.
transport: National Railways of Zimbabwe (NRZ); modernized Beitbridge Border Post (busiest land port in Southern Africa); Robert Gabriel Mugabe International Airport modern terminal.
airports: Robert Gabriel Mugabe International Airport (HRE in Harare)
Joshua Mqabuko Nkomo International Airport (BUQ in Bulawayo)
ports: Landlocked; primary oceanic freight access through Port of Beira and Port of Maputo (Mozambique), and Port of Durban (South Africa)
cuisine: Sadza (thick white cornmeal porridge, the staple foundation of every Zimbabwean meal) served with Nyama (braised beef, chicken, or goat stew) and Muriwo (steamed collard greens or mustard greens with peanut butter), Mopane Worms (Madora / Amacimbi: protein-rich crispy fried or stewed caterpillars seasoned with chili and tomatoes), Kapenta fish, Biltong, Mazondo (slow-cooked cow trotters in rich gelatinous broth), Roasted maize cobs, Maheu (fermented sweet malted corn beverage).
festivals: HIFA (Harare International Festival of the Arts)
Victoria Falls Carnival (spectacular New Year music festival)
music: Mbira dzaVadzimu (ancient thumb piano music with gourd resonator, sacred to Shona spiritual ceremonies), Chimurenga music (political liberation folk music pioneered by Thomas Mapfumo), Tuku Music (acoustic Afro-jazz developed by Oliver Mtukudzi), Sungura (fast guitar dance rhythm: Alick Macheso), Zimdancehall (immensely popular township youth genre: Winky D, Killer T).
dance: Muchongoyo warrior dance, Jerusarema / Mbende dance (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: sensual, energetic fertility and war dance with rapid footwork), Dinhe dance.
art: Shona Stone Sculpture (world-renowned contemporary art movement: serpentine stone sculptures by Nicholas Mukomberanwa, Dominic Benhura, Henry Munyaradzi, exhibited in MoMA and global museums), basket weaving (Binga baskets).
architecture: Great Zimbabwe Monument (colossal 11th-century dry-stone royal city with the Great Enclosure and Conical Tower built without mortar); Eastgate Centre in Harare (architectural masterpiece of biomimicry designed by Mick Pearce to mimic termite mounds for natural cooling without air conditioning).
literature: Superpower of African literature: Dambudzo Marechera (The House of Hunger, Guardian Fiction Prize winner), Tsitsi Dangarembga (Nervous Conditions, This Mournable Body, Booker Prize finalist), Charles Mungoshi, NoViolet Bulawayo (We Need New Names, Glory, double Booker Prize finalist), Yvonne Vera.
cinema: Neria (highest-grossing film in Zimbabwean history, soundtrack by Oliver Mtukudzi), Flame; emerging film talent at the Zimbabwe International Film Festival.
sports: Cricket (The Chevrons: passionate test-playing nation packing Harare Sports Club), Football (The Warriors: multi-time AFCON participants; Peter Ndlovu, Khama Billiat, Marvelous Nakamba), Swimming (Kirsty Coventry, Africa's most decorated Olympian with 7 Olympic medals, currently Minister of Sports and IOC member), Rugby Union (Sables).
media: The Herald, The Chronicle, NewsDay, Daily News, ZBC (Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation).
clothing: Traditional printed national fabric featuring the Zimbabwe Bird and Great Zimbabwe chevron patterns; tailored European business suits; casual wear.
holidays: February 21 (Robert Gabriel Mugabe National Youth Day)
crafts: Shona serpentine stone carvings, Binga handwoven ilala palm baskets, wooden sculptures, beadwork.
worldHeritageSites: Mana Pools National Park, Sapi and Chewore Safari Areas
Matobo Hills (sacred granite kopjes and rock art)

Mbira musical tradition and performance
flagDescription: Seven horizontal stripes of green (agriculture and rural areas), yellow (mineral wealth), red (blood shed during the Chimurenga wars of liberation), and black (the indigenous majority), with a white isosceles triangle on the hoist side (peace) bordered in black, charged with a red five-pointed star (socialism and national aspirations) overlaid with the golden Zimbabwe Bird (national emblem derived from soapstone carvings found at Great Zimbabwe).
coatOfArmsDescription: Features two kudus supporting a green shield displaying the Great Zimbabwe stone wall, an AK-47 rifle and hoe, a pick and shovel, surmounted by the golden Zimbabwe Bird on a red star, resting on a base depicting agricultural crops and cotton over the motto 'Unity, Freedom, Work'.
travelNotes: A land of breathtaking geological and archaeological majesty; Victoria Falls and Great Zimbabwe are two of the greatest sights in Africa; people are exceptionally educated, courteous, and welcoming.
shortSummary: Zimbabwe is a majestic land named after the mortarless medieval stone palaces of Great Zimbabwe, famed worldwide for the thunderous cascades of Victoria Falls, the sacred chiming notes of the Mbira, Africa's premier lithium reserves, and world-renowned Shona stone sculptures.
geography: Highest point: Mount Nyangani (2,592 m in the Eastern Highlands). Lowest point: Confluence of Runde and Save Rivers (162 m). Longest river: Zambezi River (forms northern border) / Limpopo River (southern border) / Save River. Climate: Subtropical highland climate across high plateau (Highveld) with warm wet summers (November–March) and cool dry winters (May–August); hot semi-arid in low-lying Zambezi and Limpopo valleys (Lowveld). economy: Sectors: Agriculture & Forestry 12%, Mining & Heavy Industry 25%, Services 63%. Natural resources: Lithium (largest reserves in Africa), Platinum group metals (PGMs, world #2), Gold, Chromite, Diamonds, Coal (Hwange), Nickel, Arable fertile Highveld soils. Major exports: Flue-cured tobacco, Lithium concentrates and spodumene, Gold bullion, Platinum and palladium concentrates, Ferrochrome and nickel, Diamonds.
